analysis.one_liner: Lets gig companies provide pandemic-era worker benefits without those benefits counting toward making workers employees.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let companies like Lyft, DoorDash, and Airbnb give gig workers pandemic-era help — cash assistance, health benefits, protective equipment, health checks, and COVID testing — without that help being used as evidence that the workers are actually employees. The protection applied retroactively to March 15, 2020 and ran through the later of the end of 2021 or the end of the COVID-19 public health emergency. The Senate committee it was sent to never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Gig workers — drivers, delivery couriers, and others doing jobs through apps — could have received cash help when they couldn't work for health or safety reasons, plus health benefits, protective equipment, medical supplies, health checks, and COVID testing from the companies they work through. The companies themselves would also have gained clear legal cover: none of that help could be used under any federal, state, or local law to argue their workers are employees or that the company is a joint employer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig workers, if companies opted in

how_it_helps.text: Let digital marketplace companies give cash help to gig workers who couldn't work because of health or safety concerns, without risking that the payment would later be used to classify those workers as employees.

Allowed companies to directly provide health-related benefits, protective equipment, cleaning and medical supplies, health checks, medical testing, and safety training to gig workers, and to take any action intended to protect public health.
Applied retroactively to March 15, 2020, so assistance companies had already provided during the pandemic's first waves would have been protected from use in worker-classification disputes.

analysis.who_pays: No public money was spent. The trade-off fell on gig workers pursuing misclassification claims: during the covered period — reaching back to March 2020 — the listed company actions could not be used as evidence of employment under any federal, state, or local law, which narrowed the facts workers could cite when arguing they deserved employee status and its protections like minimum wage and overtime. State and federal labor regulators likewise lost an evidentiary tool for that window.

drawbacks.text: No company had to provide anything: every benefit in the bill was voluntary, so gig workers would have had no guaranteed help even if it had passed.

The legal shield cut against workers: during the covered period, these actions could not be used as evidence of employment under any federal, state, or local law — including claims reaching back to March 2020 — narrowing gig workers' ability to argue they are employees entitled to minimum wage, overtime, and other protections.

It was temporary, expiring at the end of 2021 or when the COVID-19 public health emergency ended, whichever came later, so it addressed a snapshot of the crisis rather than the standing question of whether gig workers should get benefits as a matter of right.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered platforms legal cover to help workers during a crisis, and some companies were holding back benefits precisely because of classification risk. But the guaranteed beneficiary was the platforms' independent-contractor model: the shield was unconditional and retroactive, while the worker benefit depended entirely on voluntary company action. It was a narrow, temporary trade-off rather than a clear win for workers, and an honest supporter would have to acknowledge that it weakened the evidentiary record in exactly the disputes — employee versus contractor — that matter most to gig workers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate health committee without ever getting a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the bill on February 22, 2021, with Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina as the other initial sponsor; two Senate Republicans cosponsored in total, and no Democrat did.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig workers kept the ability to cite any company benefits as evidence in employee-classification disputes, since no shield was ever enacted. Platforms gained nothing, but also had no new obligations; the status quo simply carried over.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gig workers' classification claims stayed intact

for.name: Sen. Tim Scott
for.what_they_did: Joined as the other initial sponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 2 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Senate Democrat cosponsored it.

against.name: Sen. Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — after it was referred on the day of introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors and both cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled HELP Committee never acted, and no vote was ever recorded, so no partisan split on the merits can be measured.

industries.industry: Gig economy platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, home-sharing apps)
industries.note: The bill gave these companies a legal shield for benefits provided during the COVID emergency, removing the deterrent of that help being used to reclassify their workers as employees. That helped workers get assistance in the moment, but the same shield protected the independent-contractor model that keeps gig workers outside minimum wage, overtime, and benefits law.

The bill barred use of the covered company actions as evidence under any federal, state, or local law, including state worker-classification tests, leaving regulators with fewer facts to work with for the covered period.
